name: Lutheran Reformation
notes: Reformation movement initiated by Martin Luther in 1517.
summary: The reforming movement associated with Martin Luther and the emergence of confessionally Lutheran churches.
formation_narrative: Luther’s controversy over indulgences expanded into disputes about salvation, authority, and church practice. Reform was transmitted through preaching, vernacular teaching, print, and political protection. The 1517 date is a conventional opening milestone; regional churches took institutional form over subsequent decades. The movement did not produce one worldwide denomination, and later Lutheran churches developed different political and confessional arrangements.
core_beliefs: Justification by grace through faith: reconciliation with God is received through Christ rather than earned by religious merit.
Word and sacraments: preaching, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper are central ways in which the church communicates God’s promise.
Confessional teaching: the Augsburg Confession and catechisms explain Lutheran readings of Scripture, though bodies differ in how they subscribe to the wider Book of Concord.

key_documents.title: Book of Concord
key_documents.significance: A collection of Lutheran confessional texts consolidating the tradition after Luther; not every regional church adopted every component identically.

profile_scope: This is an introductory profile. It distinguishes shared teaching from historical development; sources do not imply that every member held an identical position. No formal corporate dissolution is asserted for this historical process. The status is unknown at the institutional level; the ending narrative explains its diffusion or development.
ending_narrative: The reforming era developed into enduring Lutheran churches and confessional traditions. It had no single corporate dissolution; churches in different territories and countries followed different institutional paths. The regional nodes are outcomes of the movement rather than members of one universal terminal merger.

name: German Lutheran territorial churches
notes: Territorial Lutheran churches in German lands following the Reformation.
summary: An aggregate of regional Lutheran churches shaped by the Reformation and the political structure of German territories.
formation_narrative: Princes and civic governments helped organize Lutheran worship, schools, and ministry in different German lands. Political settlements such as the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 shaped the setting in which territorial churches developed. This node groups multiple churches rather than naming one denomination founded that year. Emigration later carried several of these traditions to North America, where churches adopted new organizational forms.

profile_scope: The 1555 marker is not a common founding date. This aggregate still needs a territory-by-territory historical expansion.
ending_narrative: The churches in this aggregate followed different paths through political change, union, migration, and modern church organization. No single ending or successor applies to the whole group. The LCMS is one American church with relevant immigrant ancestry, not the legal successor to every German territorial church.

name: Scandinavian Lutheran state churches
notes: Lutheran state churches established in Scandinavia in the Reformation era.
summary: A regional grouping of northern European churches that adopted Lutheran reform under different national settlements.
formation_narrative: Lutheran reform entered Scandinavian kingdoms through preaching, teaching, and royal action. The resulting churches retained different national histories and forms of oversight. The dataset’s 1536 marker should not imply that all Scandinavian churches were founded or reformed simultaneously. Migration connected these national traditions to American Lutheran communities, especially through bodies that later entered the ELCA.

profile_scope: This is an aggregate, not one denomination. The exact national reform dates, leaders, and adoption histories remain a stated research gap rather than a claim of simultaneous formation.
ending_narrative: The national churches continue in differing relationships to state and society; some ceased to be established churches without ceasing to exist. Migration also contributed to American Lutheran bodies. The ELCA is therefore a related outcome of immigrant histories, not a terminal successor to all Scandinavian churches.
